rule: RFC 8785 §3.2.2.3 — numbers equivalent to an integer serialize without fraction/exponent
divergence_trap: A naive implementation that does not run ES6 Number.prototype.toString-equivalent may emit {"a":1,"b":1.0} because it preserves the lexical form from the source string.

rule: RFC 8785 §3.2.2.3 (combined with §3.2.2.4) — no representation of negative zero is allowed; must serialize as 0
divergence_trap: Most JSON parsers preserve the signedness of zero and a naive stringifier (or a parser that uses IEEE-754 .isNegative()) will emit -0, which JCS explicitly forbids.

rule: RFC 8785 §3.2.2.4 — numbers in the inclusive range [-(2^53)+1, (2^53)-1] serialize without loss; above that, the canonical JSON serialization rules of ES6 (Number.prototype.toString) apply, which uses exponent form.
divergence_trap: Implementers often cap at 2^53 and either error, round, or stringify via toFixed; values at and beyond 2^53 in JCS are emitted in shortest round-trippable form (here all four round-trip exactly because they are all representable integers in IEEE-754 doubles — the boundary is 2^53+1=9007199254740993, which is also exactly representable). The trap: 9007199254740995 is NOT exactly representable in IEEE next double after 9007199254740993 is 9007199254740996), so ES6 toString emits '9007199254740996' for 9007199254740995; a naive implementation that prints the literal 9007199254740995 will diverge from reference.

rule: RFC 8785 §3.2.2.4 — ES6 Number.prototype.toString: below 1e21 use plain integer form; 1e21 and above use exponent form; small numbers use shortest round-trip form.
divergence_trap: The cutoff in ES6 is exactly 1e21 — 1e21 prints as '1000000000000000000000' (no exponent), while 1e22 prints as '1e22'. A naive stringifier that uses toFixed or sprintf("%g") may emit '1e+21' (with explicit plus) or pick a different cutoff (e.g. printf %g uses 1e7/1e-7 boundaries), diverging badly.

rule: RFC 8785 §3.2.2.4 — numbers must be serialized as their shortest round-trippable IEEE-754 representation via ES6 Number.prototype.toString.
divergence_trap: Many implementations use toFixed(17) or printf %.17g, producing '1.0000000000000002' for 1.1 and '0.10000000000000001' for 0.1; ES6 toString yields the shortest form. Also, 1.0000000000000001 is NOT a distinct double, it equals 1.0000000000000002 in IEEE-754 — so naive lexical preservation will output '1.0000000000000001' which is wrong.

rule: RFC 8785 §3.2.2.2 — only \b, \t, \n, \f, \r, \", \\, \/ (optionally) and \uXXXX for control characters are escaped; other printable Unicode is passed through literally.
divergence_trap: The solidus '/' is escapable per the JSON spec but JCS leaves it unescaped by default; naive Python json.dumps uses ensure_ascii=True and escapes \u00xx for non-ASCII (and may or may not escape /), while json.dumps(..., ensure_ascii=False) diverges from a normalizer that escapes ASCII control chars as \u00XX (RFC requires \b \t \n \f \r forms, not \u0008 \u0009 etc.).

rule: RFC 8785 §3.2.2.2 — strings are sequences of UTF-16 code units; no Unicode normalization is performed; surrogate pairs are passed through as-is.
divergence_trap: Implementations that normalize to NFC/NFD or that escape non-BMP characters to \uD834\uDD1E will differ; Python with ensure_ascii=True will emit \uD834\uDD1E, which is identical but lexically longer — for this test the byte sequence must be the raw UTF-8 of the paired surrogate. A naive .normalize('NFC') call would yield the same here (no decomposition) but for accented Latin text would diverge by changing byte length.

rule: RFC 8785 §3.2.3 — object members are sorted by UTF-16 code unit values of their keys (lexicographic ascending), NOT by Unicode code point.
divergence_trap: UTF-16 code-unit ordering of U+E000 is 0xE000 (= 57344), and U+10000 (𐀀) is encoded as the surrogate pair 0xD800 0xDC00, whose FIRST code unit 0xD800 (= 55296) is LESS than 0xE000. So '𐀀' (0xD800,0xDC00) sorts BEFORE '' (0xE000) under JCS, but by Unicode code point U+10000 (65536) sorts AFTER U+E000 (57344). Naive sorted-keys implementations that compare decoded code points (Python str.__lt__ over full strings, or ICU collators, or Arrays.sort on JS strings) order by UTF-16 code unit already — but implementations that decode first (e.g. Python's bytes vs str with .encode().decode() with surrogate-passing, or anything using ICU's UCharIterator with code-point semantics) will invert the order of these two keys.

rule: RFC 8785 §3.2.3 / §3.2.4 — empty containers serialize to '{}' and '[]' respectively; arrays preserve index order.
divergence_trap: Some canonicalizers emit whitespace; some canonicalizers sort object keys in empty objects (no-op); arrays must never be reordered. Pair with [] test below.

rule: RFC 8785 §3.2.4 — array elements are kept in original order; object keys recursively sorted by UTF-16 code unit order (§3.2.3).
divergence_trap: Naive implementations that recursively sort both arrays and objects (a common bug) emit [1,2,3,...] for the inner array. Some implementations also mis-sort keys inside deeply nested objects (e.g. only sort top-level).

rule: RFC 8785 §3.2.3 / §3 — duplicate member names are not allowed; a conforming implementation MUST reject. This vector lists the legal deterministic outcome IF one chooses last-wins for graceful handling, but the SPEC requires rejection.
divergence_trap: Most naive canonicalizers silently pick one (often last-wins, but Python's json treats this as undefined-parse-time-error — actually a duplicate key in a JSON object is implementation-defined per RFC 8259). A reference JCS library must raise; if it doesn't, it is non-conformant. This vector is a NEGATIVE test: a reference implementation should produce an error, and a gate test should detect the absence of that error.

rule: RFC 8785 §3.2.2.2 — slash not escaped (JCS); printable Unicode (including non-ASCII) passed through literally; U+0001 is a C0 control and must escape as \u0001 (not as the literal control byte).
divergence_trap: Implementations differ on: (1) escaping '/' — JSON.stringify in older browsers escaped it; (2) whether to escape non-ASCII to \uXXXX — Python json.dumps default (ensure_ascii=True) escapes 'é' to '\u00e9'; (3) whether U+0001 serializes as the literal byte 0x01 (invalid UTF-8 in JSON) or as '\u0001' — JCS mandates '\u0001'.
